newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel noncommittal on size of solidarity tax cut.
newsitem.headline: Waigel noncommittal on size of solidarity tax cut.

text.p: Finance Minister Theo Waigel promised on Monday to cut Germany's solidarity surcharge in 1998, but avoided backing a demand by his liberal coalition partners for a two-point cut in the unpopular tax.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl's three-party coalition government agreed on Friday to put off a cut in the solidarity tax planned for next year to help shore up state finances after Waigel's tax bill was wrecked by the opposition Social Democrats (SPD).

But a coalition row broke out over the weekend over the size of the cut. Kohl's CDU said the solidarity charge should be cut by one point to 6.5 percent, but junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP) want a two-point drop.
"There are clear agreements, and they will stick," Waigel told reporters in Munich, but he declined to say how much he thought the solidarity charge should fall.
Waigel said last week that Germany would fulfil the Maastricht Treaty's terms next year to qualify for European economic and monetary union.

The Free Democrat Party (FDP) has won votes in regional polls this year by profiling itself as a tax-cutting party, and last week blocked a hike in petrol taxes originally floated by Waigel's Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU).

Waigel said that, despite the difficult tax talks, there was "at no time" any suggestion that the Kohl coalition would collapse. Kohl, speaking on Monday at his CDU's annual party conference, gave Waigel his backing and said he wanted to lead the alliance to re-election in 1998.
But the FDP kept up its attacks on Waigel on Monday, refusing further concessions on cutting the solidarity charge.
General Secretary Guido Westerwelle accused Waigel's CSU of being "an ever-greater troublemaker", and said Waigel would have more time for budget policy if he brought order to his party ranks.
The SPD, which had wielded its majority in the upper house of parliament to block key parts of Waigel's tax plans, also laid into the embattled finance minister.
Oskar Lafontaine, head of the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), said Kohl should take responsibility for the government breaking its word on tax policy instead of putting others in the firing line.
"The coalition is stumbling from one tax lie to another," he said after a party meeting in Berlin. "It has gambled away all its credit and become a burden for Germany."
